figures.alt: Map of eastern New France from 1744, showing the St. Lawrence River and Gulf, Newfoundland, Labrador, and Hudson Bay, with Native peoples named across a vast interior
figures.caption: Bellin's map of eastern New France (1744)

primary_sources: Jacques-Nicolas Bellin, Carte de la partie orientale de la Nouvelle France ou du Canada (1744)

parts.modelAnswer: One thing the map shows is that France claimed a vast territory: its title names the eastern part of New France or Canada, and the map stretches from the St. Lawrence and the Gulf across to Hudson Bay. The claim covers rivers, bays, and a great interior, far beyond the few French settlements along the St. Lawrence.
parts.prompt: Identify one thing the map shows about French claims in North America.

scoring.criterion: Earns the point for naming one accurate feature of the French claim, such as its vast size, the St. Lawrence and Hudson Bay, or the title claiming the region as New France.
scoring.notEarned: Naming only that the map shows North America, with no feature of the French claim, does not earn the point.

parts.modelAnswer: The map shows French colonization differed from English colonization because it claimed the interior through rivers and trade rather than settling the coast with farms. English colonies hugged the Atlantic shore with towns and fields, while the French map names Native peoples across a wide interior it crossed by canoe and trading post.
parts.prompt: Explain how the map shows that French colonization differed from English colonization.

scoring.criterion: Earns the point for explaining one accurate difference, such as French river and trade routes through the interior versus English coastal farming settlements.
scoring.notEarned: Stating only that the French and English were different, with no difference shown by the map, does not earn the point.

parts.modelAnswer: One limit of the map is that a claim on paper is not control on the ground: the interior it names was lived in and governed by Native peoples, and French posts there were few and small. The map shows what France wanted the world to see, not how much of the interior it actually ruled.
parts.prompt: Explain one limit of the map as evidence of who controlled the interior of North America.

scoring.criterion: Earns the point for explaining one accurate limit, such as a map claim not proving control, Native peoples still governing the interior, or few French posts on the ground.
scoring.notEarned: Stating only that maps can be wrong, with no limit tied to control of the interior, does not earn the point.

stimulus.text: Jacques-Nicolas Bellin's map of the eastern part of New France or Canada, published in 1744. The map shows the St. Lawrence River and Gulf, Newfoundland, Labrador, and Hudson Bay, with Native peoples named across a vast interior. Its title claims the whole region as New France or Canada.
